<Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez>: Digital tools are critical for workplaces of all kinds, including small businesses, and they require the use of cybersecurity and cyber hygiene infrastructure, systems and practices. According to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, 99 percent of small businesses use at least one technology platform, with 58 percent using at least four platforms. However, only 25 percent of small businesses use cybersecurity and malware detection tools. Unlike larger corporations, small business entrepreneurs and their staff lack the time, skills, and resources to adopt effective cybersecurity measures.
Multiple federal entities have developed and provided cybersecurity resources for small businesses. However, the Committee has heard feedback that awareness of these resources varies. While some federal agencies have created cybersecurity resources, it can be difficult for them to reach small businesses when those agencies lack the network and experience to perform effective small business outreach and counseling, as the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) does. The SBA, in consultation with other relevant federal entities, could be better utilized to provide assistance to small businesses on cybersecurity and technology use and adaptation, as well as disseminating information and resources.
One area of interest for small business government contractors is the cybersecurity standards and requirements that must be met to be eligible to receive a federal contract. Since 2019, the Department of Defense (DoD) has attempted to issue new cybersecurity regulations, known as the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) for defense contractors. CMMC sets a cybersecurity standard designed to ensure contractors have adequate security practices and processes in place to safeguard controlled information.
After years of mixed signals and delays, DoD formally established CMMC in a 2024 DoD rule.\1\ CMMC requires DoD prime- and sub-contractors to achieve and maintain a level of cyber hygiene and obtain a CMMC certification prior to contract award. The cost to the industrial base and the costs for each defense contractor are significant, reoccurring and vary based on level of certification needed.
\1\89 Fed. Reg. 83092 (2024).
To assist small businesses with understanding and complying with the requirements of CMMC and similar DoD regulations, Congress has authorized programs within DoD's Office of Small Business Programs and APEX Accelerators that provide resources such as assessment tools, counseling assistance and educational opportunities for small federal contractors.\2\
\2\See, e.g., Cyber Thursdays, Wis. Procurement Inst., https:// www.wispro.org/wpi-events/ featured-webinars/cyber-fridays (last visited Sep. 9, 2026); Cyber Self Assessments, Project Spectrum, U.S. Dep't of Def., https:// www.projectspectrum.io (last visited Sep. 10, 2026).
While there is universal acceptance that cybersecurity is priority, it is also widely acknowledged that CMMC is a costly, burdensome regulation that will act as a barrier to entry for small firms seeking to enter the defense industrial base and will likely accelerate the ongoing exodus of small businesses from the federal market. Accurate and timely information will assist small firms seeking to remain competitive in the federal market.
The Amendment in the Nature of a Substitute adds language that better defines an appropriate role for the SBA in cybersecurity efforts and maximize the SBA's resources by ensuring that they supplement, rather than duplicate, existing programs that are more suited for the task.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Ranking Member.
